supporting_evidence.section_heading: Date and time functions and operators # / Date and time operators #
Date and time functions and operators # / Date and time operators #

evidence_span.text: Subtracting two datetimes produces an interval with the field-maximum leading precision and the fractional-seconds precision of the datetimes, with a minimum of six fractional digits, so timestamp1 - timestamp2 of two timestamp(9) values has the type INTERVAL DAY(9) TO SECOND(9) and keeps all nine fractional digits.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Date and time functions and operators # / Date and time operators #

evidence_span.text: Adding or subtracting a day-time interval preserves the greater fractional precision of the datetime and interval, with a minimum of three digits. For example, timestamp(3) + INTERVAL '1' DAY returns timestamp(3) , while adding INTERVAL '0.000001' SECOND returns timestamp(6) .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Date and time functions and operators # / Date and time operators #

evidence_span.text: For intervals, EXTRACT requires a field present in the qualifier. The leading field is not wrapped: hour(INTERVAL '36' HOUR) returns 36 , while the hour component of a day-leading interval remains between 0 and 23 in magnitude. day_of_month remains an alias for day on intervals.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Date and time functions and operators # / Date and time operators #

evidence_span.text: To express a datetime difference with a specific day-time qualifier, enclose its subtraction in parentheses and follow it with an interval qualifier:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Date and time functions and operators # / Date and time operators #

evidence_span.text:
(timestamp '2012-10-31 01:00' - timestamp '2012-10-30 01:00') DAY TO SECOND
-- 1 00:00:00.000000, of type interval day(2) to second(6)

(timestamp '2012-10-31 01:00' - timestamp '2012-01-01 00:00') DAY(9) TO SECOND

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Date and time functions and operators # / Date and time operators #

evidence_span.text: Both operands must be datetimes. Dates are compared as midnight timestamps. The expression inside the parentheses follows normal operator precedence and must have subtraction as its outermost operation. For example, (ts1 - (ts2 + i)) DAY(3) subtracts the adjusted second timestamp, while (ts1 - ts2 + i) DAY(3) is rejected because its outermost operation is addition. The qualifier uses the same precision rules as an interval type: an omitted leading precision is 2 , so a difference of 100 days overflows DAY but fits DAY(3) . Dropping trailing fields truncates toward zero, while reducing fractional seconds rounds with ties toward positive infinity. Overflow is checked after this conversion. Year-month (calendar) differences are not currently supported.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Date and time functions and operators # / Date and time operators #

evidence_span.text: A bare field after a SELECT expression can also be an implicit column alias. For compatibility, SELECT (a - b) day FROM t and SELECT x + (a - b) day FROM t continue to use day as an alias. This also applies to ROW field aliases and PIVOT aggregation and value aliases. Ordinary arithmetic grouping is preserved: (a - b + c) day gives the alias day to (a - b) + c . Add parentheses to select a qualified value: SELECT ((a - b) DAY) FROM t . An explicit precision or a separate alias also removes the ambiguity, as in SELECT (a - b) DAY(3) FROM t or SELECT (a - b) DAY AS elapsed FROM t . Interval literals retain their qualifiers: SELECT INTERVAL '1' DAY selects an interval value without an alias.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Data types # / Date and time # / Interval fractional-seconds precision #

evidence_span.text: A SECOND type written without a fractional precision — a column type or a cast target such as CAST(x AS INTERVAL DAY TO SECOND) — defaults to 6 (microseconds), so INTERVAL DAY TO SECOND is INTERVAL DAY(2) TO SECOND(6) . A qualifier whose trailing field is not SECOND , such as DAY TO MINUTE , has no fractional-seconds precision.

evidence_span.text: Scalar numeric casts can report the error code of the corresponding SQL conversion, including numeric overflow. evidence_span.text: Filtering during aggregation #

primary_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions #

evidence_span.text: The FILTER keyword can be used to remove rows from aggregation processing with a condition expressed using a WHERE clause. This is evaluated for each row before it is used in the aggregation and is supported for all aggregate functions.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions # / Filtering during aggregation #

evidence_span.text: aggregate_function(...) FILTER (WHERE <condition>)

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions # / Filtering during aggregation #

evidence_span.text: A common and very useful example is to use FILTER to remove nulls from consideration when using array_agg :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions # / Filtering during aggregation #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT array_agg(name) FILTER (WHERE name IS NOT NULL)
FROM region;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions # / Filtering during aggregation #

evidence_span.text: As another example, imagine you want to add a condition on the count for Iris flowers, modifying the following query:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions # / Filtering during aggregation #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT species,
       count(*) AS count
FROM iris
GROUP BY species;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions # / Filtering during aggregation #

evidence_span.text:
species    | count
-----------+-------
setosa     |   50
virginica  |   50
versicolor |   50

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions # / Filtering during aggregation #

evidence_span.text: If you just use a normal WHERE statement you lose information:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions # / Filtering during aggregation #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT species,
    count(*) AS count
FROM iris
WHERE petal_length_cm > 4
GROUP BY species;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions # / Filtering during aggregation #

evidence_span.text:
species    | count
-----------+-------
virginica  |   50
versicolor |   34

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions # / Filtering during aggregation #

evidence_span.text: Using a filter you retain all information:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions # / Filtering during aggregation #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT species,
       count(*) FILTER (where petal_length_cm > 4) AS count
FROM iris
GROUP BY species;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions # / Filtering during aggregation #

evidence_span.text:
species    | count
-----------+-------
virginica  |   50
setosa     |    0
versicolor |   34

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / JSON value constructor #

evidence_span.text: Converts a character or binary string into a JSON value. With no FORMAT clause the input is treated as JSON text; FORMAT JSON ENCODING … parses a binary input with the named character encoding. Always returns JSON ; there is no RETURNING clause.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / JSON value constructor #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT JSON('[1, 2, 3]');                                     -- JSON '[1,2,3]'
SELECT JSON(X'5B312C20322C20335D' FORMAT JSON ENCODING UTF8); -- JSON '[1,2,3]'
SELECT JSON(JSON '{"a": 1}');                                 -- JSON '{"a":1}'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / JSON value constructor #

evidence_span.text: JSON(...) has no ON ERROR clause; malformed input raises a SQL error.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / JSON value constructor #

evidence_span.text: Duplicate object keys are preserved, each with its own value, and member order follows the input. A JSON literal and json_parse() parse through the same value model, so they behave the same way:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / JSON value constructor #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT json_format(JSON('{"a": 1, "a": 2}'));  -- '{"a":1,"a":2}'
SELECT json_format(JSON '{"a": 1, "a": 2}');   -- '{"a":1,"a":2}'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / JSON value constructor #

evidence_span.text: JSON is not a reserved word, so a function named json remains callable: a qualified call such as catalog.schema.json(...) resolves to the function, and only the unqualified JSON(x) is the constructor. Other call forms, such as json() , json(x, y) , and json(DISTINCT x) , are parsed as ordinary function calls and require a matching function definition.

evidence_span.text: An outer-scope receiver is supported for member access ( o.j.foo ), subscripts ( o.j.items[0] ), item methods on a subscripted chain ( o.j.items[0].bigint() ), and the member wildcard ( o.j.* ). Item methods applied directly to a dotted member chain without an intervening subscript — e.g. o.j.foo.bigint() — are not supported on outer-scope columns; query the column locally or insert an explicit JSON_VALUE call in those cases.

evidence_span.text: Casting from NULL to JSON is not straightforward. Casting from a standalone NULL will produce SQL NULL instead of JSON 'null' . However, when casting from arrays or map containing NULL s, the produced JSON will have null s in it.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / Cast to JSON #
JSON functions and operators # / Cast from JSON #

evidence_span.text: Casting to BOOLEAN , TINYINT , SMALLINT , INTEGER , BIGINT , REAL , DOUBLE , VARCHAR , DATE or TIME is supported. Casting to ARRAY and MAP is supported when the element type of the array is one of the supported types, or when the key type of the map is VARCHAR and value type of the map is one of the supported types.

evidence_span.text: json_table #

primary_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators #

evidence_span.text: The json_table clause extracts a table from a JSON value. Use this clause to transform JSON data into a relational format, making it easier to query and analyze. Use json_table in the FROM clause of a SELECT statement to create a table from JSON data.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
JSON_TABLE(
    json_input,
    json_path [ AS path_name ]
    [ PASSING value AS parameter_name [, ...] ]
    COLUMNS (
        column_definition [, ...] )
    [ PLAN ( json_table_specific_plan )
      | PLAN DEFAULT ( json_table_default_plan ) ]
    [ { ERROR | EMPTY } ON ERROR ]
)

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: The COLUMNS clause supports the following column_definition arguments:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
column_name FOR ORDINALITY
| column_name type
    [ FORMAT JSON [ ENCODING { UTF8 | UTF16 | UTF32 } ] ]
    [ PATH json_path ]
    [ { WITHOUT | WITH { CONDITIONAL | UNCONDITIONAL } } [ ARRAY ] WRAPPER ]
    [ { KEEP | OMIT } QUOTES [ ON SCALAR STRING ] ]
    [ { ERROR | NULL | EMPTY { [ARRAY] | OBJECT } | DEFAULT expression } ON EMPTY ]
    [ { ERROR | NULL | DEFAULT expression } ON ERROR ]
| NESTED [ PATH ] json_path [ AS path_name ] COLUMNS ( column_definition [, ...] )

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: json_input is a JSON value, a character string, or a binary string. A string must contain a single JSON item.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: json_path is a string literal containing the path mode specification and the path expression. It follows the syntax rules described in JSON path syntax and semantics .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
'strict ($.price + $.tax)?(@ > 99.9)'
'lax $[0 to 1].floor()?(@ > 10)'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: In the PASSING clause, pass values as named parameters that the json_path expression can reference.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
PASSING orders.totalprice AS o_price,
        orders.tax % 10 AS o_tax

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: Use named parameters to reference the values in the path expression. Prefix named parameters with $ .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: 'lax $?(@.price > $o_price || @.tax > $o_tax)'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: You can also pass JSON values in the PASSING clause. Use FORMAT JSON to specify the format and ENCODING to specify the encoding:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
PASSING orders.json_desc FORMAT JSON AS o_desc,
        orders.binary_record FORMAT JSON ENCODING UTF16 AS o_rec

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: The json_path value is case-sensitive. The SQL identifiers are uppercase. Use quoted identifiers in the PASSING clause:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
'lax $.keyvalue()?(@.name == $KeyName).value' PASSING nation.name AS KeyName --> ERROR; no passed value found
'lax $.keyvalue()?(@.name == $KeyName).value' PASSING nation.name AS "KeyName" --> correct

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: The PLAN clause specifies how to join columns from different paths. Use OUTER or INNER to define how to join parent paths with their child paths. Use CROSS or UNION to join siblings.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: COLUMNS defines the schema of your table. Each column_definition specifies how to extract and format your json_input value into a relational column.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: PLAN is an optional clause to control how to process and join nested JSON data.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: ON ERROR specifies how to handle processing errors. ERROR ON ERROR throws an error. EMPTY ON ERROR returns an empty result set.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: For each value column with DEFAULT in its ON EMPTY or ON ERROR clause, the default expression is only evaluated when the corresponding branch is taken, and if the ON EMPTY default itself raises a data exception, the failure cascades to the ON ERROR clause. Subqueries are not supported in json_table DEFAULT expressions.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: column_name specifies a column name.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: FOR ORDINALITY adds a row number column to the output table, starting at 1 . Specify the column name in the column definition:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: row_num FOR ORDINALITY

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: NESTED PATH extracts data from nested levels of a json_input value. Each NESTED PATH clause can contain column_definition values.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: The json_table function returns a result set that you can use like any other table in your queries. You can join the result set with other tables or combine multiple arrays from your JSON data.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: You can also process nested JSON objects without parsing the data multiple times.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: Use json_table as a lateral join to process JSON data from another table.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

structural.name: JSON_TABLE

evidence_span.text: json_table #

primary_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators #

signatures: JSON_TABLE( json_input, json_path [ AS path_name ] [ PASSING value AS parameter_name [, ...] ] COLUMNS ( column_definition [, ...] )

evidence_span.text: The json_table clause extracts a table from a JSON value. Use this clause to transform JSON data into a relational format, making it easier to query and analyze. Use json_table in the FROM clause of a SELECT statement to create a table from JSON data.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
JSON_TABLE(
    json_input,
    json_path [ AS path_name ]
    [ PASSING value AS parameter_name [, ...] ]
    COLUMNS (
        column_definition [, ...] )
    [ PLAN ( json_table_specific_plan )
      | PLAN DEFAULT ( json_table_default_plan ) ]
    [ { ERROR | EMPTY } ON ERROR ]
)

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: The COLUMNS clause supports the following column_definition arguments:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
column_name FOR ORDINALITY
| column_name type
    [ FORMAT JSON [ ENCODING { UTF8 | UTF16 | UTF32 } ] ]
    [ PATH json_path ]
    [ { WITHOUT | WITH { CONDITIONAL | UNCONDITIONAL } } [ ARRAY ] WRAPPER ]
    [ { KEEP | OMIT } QUOTES [ ON SCALAR STRING ] ]
    [ { ERROR | NULL | EMPTY { [ARRAY] | OBJECT } | DEFAULT expression } ON EMPTY ]
    [ { ERROR | NULL | DEFAULT expression } ON ERROR ]
| NESTED [ PATH ] json_path [ AS path_name ] COLUMNS ( column_definition [, ...] )

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: json_input is a JSON value, a character string, or a binary string. A string must contain a single JSON item.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: json_path is a string literal containing the path mode specification and the path expression. It follows the syntax rules described in JSON path syntax and semantics .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
'strict ($.price + $.tax)?(@ > 99.9)'
'lax $[0 to 1].floor()?(@ > 10)'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: In the PASSING clause, pass values as named parameters that the json_path expression can reference.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
PASSING orders.totalprice AS o_price,
        orders.tax % 10 AS o_tax

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: Use named parameters to reference the values in the path expression. Prefix named parameters with $ .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: 'lax $?(@.price > $o_price || @.tax > $o_tax)'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: You can also pass JSON values in the PASSING clause. Use FORMAT JSON to specify the format and ENCODING to specify the encoding:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
PASSING orders.json_desc FORMAT JSON AS o_desc,
        orders.binary_record FORMAT JSON ENCODING UTF16 AS o_rec

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: The json_path value is case-sensitive. The SQL identifiers are uppercase. Use quoted identifiers in the PASSING clause:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
'lax $.keyvalue()?(@.name == $KeyName).value' PASSING nation.name AS KeyName --> ERROR; no passed value found
'lax $.keyvalue()?(@.name == $KeyName).value' PASSING nation.name AS "KeyName" --> correct

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: The PLAN clause specifies how to join columns from different paths. Use OUTER or INNER to define how to join parent paths with their child paths. Use CROSS or UNION to join siblings.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: COLUMNS defines the schema of your table. Each column_definition specifies how to extract and format your json_input value into a relational column.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: PLAN is an optional clause to control how to process and join nested JSON data.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: ON ERROR specifies how to handle processing errors. ERROR ON ERROR throws an error. EMPTY ON ERROR returns an empty result set.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: For each value column with DEFAULT in its ON EMPTY or ON ERROR clause, the default expression is only evaluated when the corresponding branch is taken, and if the ON EMPTY default itself raises a data exception, the failure cascades to the ON ERROR clause. Subqueries are not supported in json_table DEFAULT expressions.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: column_name specifies a column name.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: FOR ORDINALITY adds a row number column to the output table, starting at 1 . Specify the column name in the column definition:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: row_num FOR ORDINALITY

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: NESTED PATH extracts data from nested levels of a json_input value. Each NESTED PATH clause can contain column_definition values.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: The json_table function returns a result set that you can use like any other table in your queries. You can join the result set with other tables or combine multiple arrays from your JSON data.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: You can also process nested JSON objects without parsing the data multiple times.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: Use json_table as a lateral join to process JSON data from another table.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: Examples #

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: The following query uses json_table to extract values from a JSON array and return them as rows in a table with three columns:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table # / Examples #
JSON functions and operators # / json_table # / Examples #

evidence_span.text: id child wiki_data_id 1 Africa Q1 2 Americas Q828 3 Asia Q48 4 Europe Q51

structural.name: JSON_OBJECT

evidence_span.text: The json_object function creates a JSON object containing given key-value pairs.

primary_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object #

signatures: JSON_OBJECT( [ key_value [, ...] [ { NULL ON NULL | ABSENT ON NULL } ] ], [ { WITH UNIQUE [ KEYS ] | WITHOUT UNIQUE [ KEYS ] } ] [ RETURNING type [ FORMAT JSON [ ENCODING { UTF8 | UTF16 | UTF32 } ] ] ] )

evidence_span.text:
JSON_OBJECT(
    [ key_value [, ...]
      [ { NULL ON NULL | ABSENT ON NULL } ] ],
      [ { WITH UNIQUE [ KEYS ] | WITHOUT UNIQUE [ KEYS ] } ]
    [ RETURNING type [ FORMAT JSON [ ENCODING { UTF8 | UTF16 | UTF32 } ] ] ]
    )

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object #

evidence_span.text: Argument passing conventions #

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object #

evidence_span.text: There are two conventions for passing keys and values:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Argument passing conventions #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT json_object('key1' : 1, 'key2' : true)
--> '{"key1":1,"key2":true}'

SELECT json_object(KEY 'key1' VALUE 1, KEY 'key2' VALUE true)
--> '{"key1":1,"key2":true}'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Argument passing conventions #

evidence_span.text: In the second convention, you can omit the KEY keyword:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Argument passing conventions #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT json_object('key1' VALUE 1, 'key2' VALUE true)
--> '{"key1":1,"key2":true}'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Argument passing conventions #

evidence_span.text: Argument types #

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object #

evidence_span.text: The keys can be arbitrary expressions. They must be of character string type. Each key is converted into a JSON text item, and it becomes a key in the created JSON object. Keys must not be null.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Argument types #

evidence_span.text: You can pass SQL values of types boolean, numeric, and character string. They are converted to corresponding JSON literals:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Argument types #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT json_object('x' : true, 'y' : 12e-1, 'z' : 'text')
--> '{"x":true,"y":1.2,"z":"text"}'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Argument types #

evidence_span.text: Values of type JSON are consumed as JSON without a FORMAT clause. This also applies to JSON-typed columns and expressions. Character or binary strings require a specified format and optional encoding to be interpreted as JSON:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Argument types #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT json_object(
                   'x' : '[  "text"  ] ' FORMAT JSON,
                   'y' : X'5B0035005D00' FORMAT JSON ENCODING UTF16
                  )
--> '{"x":["text"],"y":[5]}'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Argument types #

evidence_span.text: You can also nest other JSON-returning functions. In that case, the FORMAT option is implicit:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Argument types #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT json_object(
                   'x' : json_query('{"key" : [  "value"  ]}', 'lax $.key')
                  )
--> '{"x":["value"]}'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Argument types #

evidence_span.text: Other passed values are cast to varchar, and they become JSON text literals:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Argument types #
JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Argument types #

evidence_span.text: You can omit the arguments altogether to get an empty object:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Argument types #

evidence_span.text: SELECT json_object() --> '{}'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Argument types #

evidence_span.text: Null handling #

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object #

evidence_span.text: The values passed for JSON object keys must not be null. It is allowed to pass null for JSON object values. A null value is treated according to the specified null treatment option. If NULL ON NULL is specified, a JSON object entry with null value is added to the result. If ABSENT ON NULL is specified, the entry is omitted in the result. NULL ON NULL is the default configuration.:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Null handling #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT json_object('x' : null, 'y' : 1)
--> '{"x":null,"y":1}'

SELECT json_object('x' : null, 'y' : 1 NULL ON NULL)
--> '{"x":null,"y":1}'

SELECT json_object('x' : null, 'y' : 1 ABSENT ON NULL)
--> '{"y":1}'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Null handling #

evidence_span.text: Key uniqueness #

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object #

evidence_span.text: If a duplicate key is encountered, it is handled according to the specified key uniqueness constraint.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Key uniqueness #

evidence_span.text: If WITH UNIQUE KEYS is specified, a duplicate key results in a query failure:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Key uniqueness #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT json_object('x' : null, 'x' : 1 WITH UNIQUE KEYS)
--> failure: "duplicate key passed to JSON_OBJECT function"

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Key uniqueness #

evidence_span.text: Keys are checked in every nested object, including objects inside arrays. This applies both to JSON-typed arguments and to strings supplied with FORMAT JSON . The same key can occur in separate sibling objects; uniqueness is local to each object. An argument containing duplicate keys in any one object is rejected:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Key uniqueness #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT json_object('x' : '{"a": 1, "a": 2}' FORMAT JSON WITH UNIQUE KEYS)
--> failure: "duplicate key passed to JSON_OBJECT function"

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Key uniqueness #

evidence_span.text: WITHOUT UNIQUE KEYS is the default configuration; duplicate keys are preserved in insertion order.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Key uniqueness #

evidence_span.text: Returned type #

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object #

evidence_span.text: By default, the json_object function returns varchar containing the textual representation of the JSON object. With the RETURNING clause, you can specify other character string type:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Returned type #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT json_object('x' : 1 RETURNING VARCHAR(100))
--> '{"x":1}'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Returned type #

evidence_span.text: You can also specify to use varbinary and the required encoding as return type. The default encoding is UTF8:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Returned type #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT json_object('x' : 1 RETURNING VARBINARY)
--> X'7b 22 78 22 3a 31 7d'

SELECT json_object('x' : 1 RETURNING VARBINARY FORMAT JSON ENCODING UTF8)
--> X'7b 22 78 22 3a 31 7d'

SELECT json_object('x' : 1 RETURNING VARBINARY FORMAT JSON ENCODING UTF16)
--> X'7b 00 22 00 78 00 22 00 3a 00 31 00 7d 00'

SELECT json_object('x' : 1 RETURNING VARBINARY FORMAT JSON ENCODING UTF32)
--> X'7b 00 00 00 22 00 00 00 78 00 00 00 22 00 00 00 3a 00 00 00 31 00 00 00 7d 00 00 00'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Returned type #

evidence_span.text: Warning

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Returned type #

evidence_span.text: The following functions and operators are not compliant with the SQL standard, and should be considered deprecated. According to the SQL standard, there shall be no JSON data type. Instead, JSON values should be represented as string values. The remaining functionality of the following functions is covered by the functions described previously.

primary_evidence.section_heading: HyperLogLog functions #

evidence_span.text: Trino implements HyperLogLog data sketches as a set of 32-bit buckets which store a maximum hash . They can be stored sparsely (as a map from bucket ID to bucket), or densely (as a contiguous memory block). The HyperLogLog data structure starts as the sparse representation, switching to dense when it is more efficient. The P4HyperLogLog structure is initialized densely and remains dense for its lifetime.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / JSON value constructor #

evidence_span.text: Converts a character or binary string into a JSON value. With no FORMAT clause the input is treated as JSON text; FORMAT JSON ENCODING … parses a binary input with the named character encoding. Always returns JSON ; there is no RETURNING clause.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / JSON value constructor #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT JSON('[1, 2, 3]');                                     -- JSON '[1,2,3]'
SELECT JSON(X'5B312C20322C20335D' FORMAT JSON ENCODING UTF8); -- JSON '[1,2,3]'
SELECT JSON(JSON '{"a": 1}');                                 -- JSON '{"a":1}'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / JSON value constructor #

evidence_span.text: json_value #

primary_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators #

evidence_span.text: The json_value function extracts a scalar SQL value from a JSON value.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text:
JSON_VALUE(
    json_input [ FORMAT JSON [ ENCODING { UTF8 | UTF16 | UTF32 } ] ],
    json_path
    [ PASSING json_argument [, ...] ]
    [ RETURNING type ]
    [ { ERROR | NULL | DEFAULT expression } ON EMPTY ]
    [ { ERROR | NULL | DEFAULT expression } ON ERROR ]
    )

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: The json_path is evaluated using the json_input as the context variable ( $ ), and the passed arguments as the named variables ( $variable_name ).

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: The returned value is the SQL scalar returned by the path. By default, it is converted to string ( varchar ). In the RETURNING clause, you can specify other desired type: a character string type, numeric, boolean or datetime type.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: json_input is a JSON value, a character string, or a binary string. A string should contain a single JSON item; for a binary string, you can specify encoding.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: json_path is a string literal, containing the path mode specification, and the path expression, following the syntax rules described in JSON path syntax and semantics .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text:
'strict $.price + $tax'
'lax $[last].abs().floor()'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: In the PASSING clause you can pass arbitrary expressions to be used by the path expression.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: PASSING orders.tax AS O_TAX

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: The passed parameters can be referenced in the path expression by named variables, prefixed with $ .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: 'strict $[last].price + $O_TAX'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: Additionally to SQL values, you can pass JSON values, specifying the format and optional encoding:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text:
PASSING orders.json_desc FORMAT JSON AS o_desc,
        orders.binary_record FORMAT JSON ENCODING UTF16 AS o_rec

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: Note that the JSON path language is case-sensitive, while the unquoted SQL identifiers are upper-cased. Therefore, it is recommended to use quoted identifiers in the PASSING clause:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text:
'lax $.keyvalue()?(@.name == $KeyName).value' PASSING nation.name AS KeyName --> ERROR; no passed value found
'lax $.keyvalue()?(@.name == $KeyName).value' PASSING nation.name AS "KeyName" --> correct

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: If the path returns an empty sequence, the ON EMPTY clause is applied. The default value returned ON EMPTY is NULL . You can also specify the default value:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: DEFAULT -1 ON EMPTY

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: If an error occurs, the returned value depends on the ON ERROR clause. The default value returned ON ERROR is NULL . One example of error is multiple items returned by the path. Other errors caught and handled according to the ON ERROR clause are:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: Input conversion errors, such as malformed JSON

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: JSON path evaluation errors, e.g. division by zero

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: Returned scalar not convertible to the desired type

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: The DEFAULT expression in ON EMPTY and ON ERROR is only evaluated when the corresponding branch is taken. If evaluation of the ON EMPTY default itself raises a data exception, the failure cascades to the ON ERROR clause. Subqueries are not supported in DEFAULT expressions.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: Examples #

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: Let customers be a table containing two columns: id:bigint , description:varchar .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value # / Examples #

evidence_span.text: id description 101 ‘{“comment” : “nice”, “children” : [10, 13, 16]}’ 102 ‘{“comment” : “problematic”, “children” : [8, 11]}’ 103 ‘{“comment” : “knows best”, “children” : [2]}’

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value # / Examples #

evidence_span.text: json_table #

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators #

evidence_span.text: The json_table clause extracts a table from a JSON value. Use this clause to transform JSON data into a relational format, making it easier to query and analyze. Use json_table in the FROM clause of a SELECT statement to create a table from JSON data.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
JSON_TABLE(
    json_input,
    json_path [ AS path_name ]
    [ PASSING value AS parameter_name [, ...] ]
    COLUMNS (
        column_definition [, ...] )
    [ PLAN ( json_table_specific_plan )
      | PLAN DEFAULT ( json_table_default_plan ) ]
    [ { ERROR | EMPTY } ON ERROR ]
)

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: The COLUMNS clause supports the following column_definition arguments:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
column_name FOR ORDINALITY
| column_name type
    [ FORMAT JSON [ ENCODING { UTF8 | UTF16 | UTF32 } ] ]
    [ PATH json_path ]
    [ { WITHOUT | WITH { CONDITIONAL | UNCONDITIONAL } } [ ARRAY ] WRAPPER ]
    [ { KEEP | OMIT } QUOTES [ ON SCALAR STRING ] ]
    [ { ERROR | NULL | EMPTY { [ARRAY] | OBJECT } | DEFAULT expression } ON EMPTY ]
    [ { ERROR | NULL | DEFAULT expression } ON ERROR ]
| NESTED [ PATH ] json_path [ AS path_name ] COLUMNS ( column_definition [, ...] )

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: json_input is a JSON value, a character string, or a binary string. A string must contain a single JSON item.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: json_path is a string literal containing the path mode specification and the path expression. It follows the syntax rules described in JSON path syntax and semantics .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
'strict ($.price + $.tax)?(@ > 99.9)'
'lax $[0 to 1].floor()?(@ > 10)'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: In the PASSING clause, pass values as named parameters that the json_path expression can reference.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
PASSING orders.totalprice AS o_price,
        orders.tax % 10 AS o_tax

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: Use named parameters to reference the values in the path expression. Prefix named parameters with $ .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: 'lax $?(@.price > $o_price || @.tax > $o_tax)'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: You can also pass JSON values in the PASSING clause. Use FORMAT JSON to specify the format and ENCODING to specify the encoding:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
PASSING orders.json_desc FORMAT JSON AS o_desc,
        orders.binary_record FORMAT JSON ENCODING UTF16 AS o_rec

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: The json_path value is case-sensitive. The SQL identifiers are uppercase. Use quoted identifiers in the PASSING clause:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
'lax $.keyvalue()?(@.name == $KeyName).value' PASSING nation.name AS KeyName --> ERROR; no passed value found
'lax $.keyvalue()?(@.name == $KeyName).value' PASSING nation.name AS "KeyName" --> correct

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: The PLAN clause specifies how to join columns from different paths. Use OUTER or INNER to define how to join parent paths with their child paths. Use CROSS or UNION to join siblings.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: COLUMNS defines the schema of your table. Each column_definition specifies how to extract and format your json_input value into a relational column.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: PLAN is an optional clause to control how to process and join nested JSON data.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: ON ERROR specifies how to handle processing errors. ERROR ON ERROR throws an error. EMPTY ON ERROR returns an empty result set.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: For each value column with DEFAULT in its ON EMPTY or ON ERROR clause, the default expression is only evaluated when the corresponding branch is taken, and if the ON EMPTY default itself raises a data exception, the failure cascades to the ON ERROR clause. Subqueries are not supported in json_table DEFAULT expressions.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: column_name specifies a column name.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: FOR ORDINALITY adds a row number column to the output table, starting at 1 . Specify the column name in the column definition:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: row_num FOR ORDINALITY

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: NESTED PATH extracts data from nested levels of a json_input value. Each NESTED PATH clause can contain column_definition values.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: The json_table function returns a result set that you can use like any other table in your queries. You can join the result set with other tables or combine multiple arrays from your JSON data.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: You can also process nested JSON objects without parsing the data multiple times.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: Use json_table as a lateral join to process JSON data from another table.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: Examples #

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: The following query uses json_table to extract values from a JSON array and return them as rows in a table with three columns:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table # / Examples #
JSON functions and operators # / json_table # / Examples #

evidence_span.text: id child wiki_data_id 1 Africa Q1 2 Americas Q828 3 Asia Q48 4 Europe Q51

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table # / Examples #

WITH UNCONDITIONAL ARRAY WRAPPER wraps every result. | JSON functions and operators # json_query #

evidence_span.text: json_query #

primary_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators #

evidence_span.text: The json_query function extracts a JSON value from a JSON value.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_query #

evidence_span.text:
JSON_QUERY(
    json_input [ FORMAT JSON [ ENCODING { UTF8 | UTF16 | UTF32 } ] ],
    json_path
    [ PASSING json_argument [, ...] ]
    [ RETURNING type [ FORMAT JSON [ ENCODING { UTF8 | UTF16 | UTF32 } ] ] ]
    [ WITHOUT [ ARRAY ] WRAPPER |
      WITH [ { CONDITIONAL | UNCONDITIONAL } ] [ ARRAY ] WRAPPER ]
    [ { KEEP | OMIT } QUOTES [ ON SCALAR STRING ] ]
    [ { ERROR | NULL | EMPTY ARRAY | EMPTY OBJECT } ON EMPTY ]
    [ { ERROR | NULL | EMPTY ARRAY | EMPTY OBJECT } ON ERROR ]
    )

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_query #

evidence_span.text: The constant string json_path is evaluated using the json_input as the context variable ( $ ), and the passed arguments as the named variables ( $variable_name ).

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_query #

evidence_span.text: The returned value is a JSON item returned by the path. With no RETURNING clause it is a JSON value when the input is JSON -typed, and a character string ( varchar ) otherwise. In the RETURNING clause, you can specify another character string type or varbinary . With varbinary , you can also specify the desired encoding.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_query #

evidence_span.text: json_input is a JSON value, a character string, or a binary string. A string should contain a single JSON item; for a binary string, you can specify encoding.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_query #

evidence_span.text: json_path is a string literal, containing the path mode specification, and the path expression, following the syntax rules described in JSON path syntax and semantics .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_query #

evidence_span.text:
'strict $.keyvalue()?(@.name == $cust_id)'
'lax $[5 to last]'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_query #

evidence_span.text: In the PASSING clause you can pass arbitrary expressions to be used by the path expression.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_query #

evidence_span.text: PASSING orders.custkey AS CUST_ID

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_query #

evidence_span.text: The passed parameters can be referenced in the path expression by named variables, prefixed with $ .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_query #

evidence_span.text: 'strict $.keyvalue()?(@.value == $CUST_ID)'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_query #

evidence_span.text: Additionally to SQL values, you can pass JSON values, specifying the format and optional encoding:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_query #

evidence_span.text:
PASSING orders.json_desc FORMAT JSON AS o_desc,
        orders.binary_record FORMAT JSON ENCODING UTF16 AS o_rec

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_query #

evidence_span.text: Note that the JSON path language is case-sensitive, while the unquoted SQL identifiers are upper-cased. Therefore, it is recommended to use quoted identifiers in the PASSING clause:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_query #

evidence_span.text:
'lax $.keyvalue()?(@.name == $KeyName).value' PASSING nation.name AS KeyName --> ERROR; no passed value found
'lax $.keyvalue()?(@.name == $KeyName).value' PASSING nation.name AS "KeyName" --> correct

WITH CONDITIONAL ARRAY WRAPPER wraps every result which is not a singleton JSON array or JSON object. WITH UNCONDITIONAL ARRAY WRAPPER wraps every result.

evidence_span.text: The QUOTES clause lets you modify the result for a scalar string by removing the double quotes being part of the JSON string representation.

evidence_span.text: Subtracting two datetimes produces an interval with the field-maximum leading precision and the fractional-seconds precision of the datetimes, with a minimum of six fractional digits, so timestamp1 - timestamp2 of two timestamp(9) values has the type INTERVAL DAY(9) TO SECOND(9) and keeps all nine fractional digits.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Date and time functions and operators # / Date and time operators #

evidence_span.text: Adding or subtracting a day-time interval preserves the greater fractional precision of the datetime and interval, with a minimum of three digits. For example, timestamp(3) + INTERVAL '1' DAY returns timestamp(3) , while adding INTERVAL '0.000001' SECOND returns timestamp(6) .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Date and time functions and operators # / Date and time operators #

evidence_span.text: For intervals, EXTRACT requires a field present in the qualifier. The leading field is not wrapped: hour(INTERVAL '36' HOUR) returns 36 , while the hour component of a day-leading interval remains between 0 and 23 in magnitude. day_of_month remains an alias for day on intervals.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Date and time functions and operators # / Date and time operators #

evidence_span.text: To express a datetime difference with a specific day-time qualifier, enclose its subtraction in parentheses and follow it with an interval qualifier:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Date and time functions and operators # / Date and time operators #

evidence_span.text:
(timestamp '2012-10-31 01:00' - timestamp '2012-10-30 01:00') DAY TO SECOND
-- 1 00:00:00.000000, of type interval day(2) to second(6)

(timestamp '2012-10-31 01:00' - timestamp '2012-01-01 00:00') DAY(9) TO SECOND

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Date and time functions and operators # / Date and time operators #

evidence_span.text: Both operands must be datetimes. Dates are compared as midnight timestamps. The expression inside the parentheses follows normal operator precedence and must have subtraction as its outermost operation. For example, (ts1 - (ts2 + i)) DAY(3) subtracts the adjusted second timestamp, while (ts1 - ts2 + i) DAY(3) is rejected because its outermost operation is addition. The qualifier uses the same precision rules as an interval type: an omitted leading precision is 2 , so a difference of 100 days overflows DAY but fits DAY(3) . Dropping trailing fields truncates toward zero, while reducing fractional seconds rounds with ties toward positive infinity. Overflow is checked after this conversion. Year-month (calendar) differences are not currently supported.

evidence_span.text: Subtracting two datetimes produces an interval with the field-maximum leading precision and the fractional-seconds precision of the datetimes, with a minimum of six fractional digits, so timestamp1 - timestamp2 of two timestamp(9) values has the type INTERVAL DAY(9) TO SECOND(9) and keeps all nine fractional digits.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Date and time functions and operators # / Date and time operators #

evidence_span.text: Adding or subtracting a day-time interval preserves the greater fractional precision of the datetime and interval, with a minimum of three digits. For example, timestamp(3) + INTERVAL '1' DAY returns timestamp(3) , while adding INTERVAL '0.000001' SECOND returns timestamp(6) .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Date and time functions and operators # / Date and time operators #

evidence_span.text: For intervals, EXTRACT requires a field present in the qualifier. The leading field is not wrapped: hour(INTERVAL '36' HOUR) returns 36 , while the hour component of a day-leading interval remains between 0 and 23 in magnitude. day_of_month remains an alias for day on intervals.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Date and time functions and operators # / Date and time operators #

evidence_span.text: To express a datetime difference with a specific day-time qualifier, enclose its subtraction in parentheses and follow it with an interval qualifier:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Date and time functions and operators # / Date and time operators #

evidence_span.text:
(timestamp '2012-10-31 01:00' - timestamp '2012-10-30 01:00') DAY TO SECOND
-- 1 00:00:00.000000, of type interval day(2) to second(6)

(timestamp '2012-10-31 01:00' - timestamp '2012-01-01 00:00') DAY(9) TO SECOND

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Date and time functions and operators # / Date and time operators #

evidence_span.text: Both operands must be datetimes. Dates are compared as midnight timestamps. The expression inside the parentheses follows normal operator precedence and must have subtraction as its outermost operation. For example, (ts1 - (ts2 + i)) DAY(3) subtracts the adjusted second timestamp, while (ts1 - ts2 + i) DAY(3) is rejected because its outermost operation is addition. The qualifier uses the same precision rules as an interval type: an omitted leading precision is 2 , so a difference of 100 days overflows DAY but fits DAY(3) . Dropping trailing fields truncates toward zero, while reducing fractional seconds rounds with ties toward positive infinity. Overflow is checked after this conversion. Year-month (calendar) differences are not currently supported.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Date and time functions and operators # / Date and time operators #

evidence_span.text: A bare field after a SELECT expression can also be an implicit column alias. For compatibility, SELECT (a - b) day FROM t and SELECT x + (a - b) day FROM t continue to use day as an alias. This also applies to ROW field aliases and PIVOT aggregation and value aliases. Ordinary arithmetic grouping is preserved: (a - b + c) day gives the alias day to (a - b) + c . Add parentheses to select a qualified value: SELECT ((a - b) DAY) FROM t . An explicit precision or a separate alias also removes the ambiguity, as in SELECT (a - b) DAY(3) FROM t or SELECT (a - b) DAY AS elapsed FROM t . Interval literals retain their qualifiers: SELECT INTERVAL '1' DAY selects an interval value without an alias.

adaptation_provenance.raw_text: A bare field after a SELECT expression can also be an implicit column alias. For compatibility, SELECT (a - b) day FROM t and SELECT x + (a - b) day FROM t continue to use day as an alias. This also applies to ROW field aliases and PIVOT aggregation and value aliases. Ordinary arithmetic grouping is preserved: (a - b + c) day gives the alias day to (a - b) + c . Add parentheses to select a qualified value: SELECT ((a - b) DAY) FROM t . An explicit precision or a separate alias also removes the ambiguity, as in SELECT (a - b) DAY(3) FROM t or SELECT (a - b) DAY AS elapsed FROM t . Interval literals retain their qualifiers: SELECT INTERVAL '1' DAY selects an interval value without an alias. | Date and time functions and operators # Date and time operators #

evidence_span.text: Subtracting two datetimes produces an interval with the field-maximum leading precision and the fractional-seconds precision of the datetimes, with a minimum of six fractional digits, so timestamp1 - timestamp2 of two timestamp(9) values has the type INTERVAL DAY(9) TO SECOND(9) and keeps all nine fractional digits.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Date and time functions and operators # / Date and time operators #

evidence_span.text: Adding or subtracting a day-time interval preserves the greater fractional precision of the datetime and interval, with a minimum of three digits. For example, timestamp(3) + INTERVAL '1' DAY returns timestamp(3) , while adding INTERVAL '0.000001' SECOND returns timestamp(6) .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Date and time functions and operators # / Date and time operators #

evidence_span.text: For intervals, EXTRACT requires a field present in the qualifier. The leading field is not wrapped: hour(INTERVAL '36' HOUR) returns 36 , while the hour component of a day-leading interval remains between 0 and 23 in magnitude. day_of_month remains an alias for day on intervals.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Date and time functions and operators # / Date and time operators #

evidence_span.text: To express a datetime difference with a specific day-time qualifier, enclose its subtraction in parentheses and follow it with an interval qualifier:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Date and time functions and operators # / Date and time operators #

evidence_span.text:
(timestamp '2012-10-31 01:00' - timestamp '2012-10-30 01:00') DAY TO SECOND
-- 1 00:00:00.000000, of type interval day(2) to second(6)

(timestamp '2012-10-31 01:00' - timestamp '2012-01-01 00:00') DAY(9) TO SECOND

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Date and time functions and operators # / Date and time operators #

evidence_span.text: Both operands must be datetimes. Dates are compared as midnight timestamps. The expression inside the parentheses follows normal operator precedence and must have subtraction as its outermost operation. For example, (ts1 - (ts2 + i)) DAY(3) subtracts the adjusted second timestamp, while (ts1 - ts2 + i) DAY(3) is rejected because its outermost operation is addition. The qualifier uses the same precision rules as an interval type: an omitted leading precision is 2 , so a difference of 100 days overflows DAY but fits DAY(3) . Dropping trailing fields truncates toward zero, while reducing fractional seconds rounds with ties toward positive infinity. Overflow is checked after this conversion. Year-month (calendar) differences are not currently supported.

evidence_span.text: json_array #

primary_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators #

evidence_span.text: The json_array function creates a JSON array containing given elements.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_array #

evidence_span.text:
JSON_ARRAY(
    [ array_element [, ...]
      [ { NULL ON NULL | ABSENT ON NULL } ] ],
    [ RETURNING type [ FORMAT JSON [ ENCODING { UTF8 | UTF16 | UTF32 } ] ] ]
    )

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_array #

evidence_span.text: Argument types #

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_array #

evidence_span.text: The array elements can be arbitrary expressions. Each passed value is converted into a JSON item according to its type, and optional FORMAT and ENCODING specification.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_array # / Argument types #

evidence_span.text: You can pass SQL values of types boolean, numeric, and character string. They are converted to corresponding JSON literals:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_array # / Argument types #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT json_array(true, 12e-1, 'text')
--> '[true,1.2,"text"]'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_array # / Argument types #

evidence_span.text: Values of type JSON are consumed as JSON without a FORMAT clause. This also applies to JSON-typed columns and expressions. Character or binary strings require a specified format and optional encoding to be interpreted as JSON:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_array # / Argument types #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT json_array(
                  '[  "text"  ] ' FORMAT JSON,
                  X'5B0035005D00' FORMAT JSON ENCODING UTF16
                 )
--> '[["text"],[5]]'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_array # / Argument types #

evidence_span.text: You can also nest other JSON-returning functions. In that case, the FORMAT option is implicit:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_array # / Argument types #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT json_array(
                  json_query('{"key" : [  "value"  ]}', 'lax $.key')
                 )
--> '[["value"]]'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_array # / Argument types #

evidence_span.text: Other passed values are cast to varchar, and they become JSON text literals:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_array # / Argument types #
JSON functions and operators # / json_array # / Argument types #

evidence_span.text: You can omit the arguments altogether to get an empty array:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_array # / Argument types #

evidence_span.text: SELECT json_array() --> '[]'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_array # / Argument types #

evidence_span.text: Null handling #

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_array #

evidence_span.text: If a value passed for an array element is null , it is treated according to the specified null treatment option. If ABSENT ON NULL is specified, the null element is omitted in the result. If NULL ON NULL is specified, JSON null is added to the result. ABSENT ON NULL is the default configuration:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_array # / Null handling #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT json_array(true, null, 1)
--> '[true,1]'

SELECT json_array(true, null, 1 ABSENT ON NULL)
--> '[true,1]'

SELECT json_array(true, null, 1 NULL ON NULL)
--> '[true,null,1]'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_array # / Null handling #

evidence_span.text: Returned type #

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_array #

evidence_span.text: By default, the json_array function returns varchar containing the textual representation of the JSON array. With the RETURNING clause, you can specify other character string type:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_array # / Returned type #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT json_array(true, 1 RETURNING VARCHAR(100))
--> '[true,1]'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_array # / Returned type #

evidence_span.text: You can also specify to use varbinary and the required encoding as return type. The default encoding is UTF8:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_array # / Returned type #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT json_array(true, 1 RETURNING VARBINARY)
--> X'5b 74 72 75 65 2c 31 5d'

SELECT json_array(true, 1 RETURNING VARBINARY FORMAT JSON ENCODING UTF8)
--> X'5b 74 72 75 65 2c 31 5d'

SELECT json_array(true, 1 RETURNING VARBINARY FORMAT JSON ENCODING UTF16)
--> X'5b 00 74 00 72 00 75 00 65 00 2c 00 31 00 5d 00'

SELECT json_array(true, 1 RETURNING VARBINARY FORMAT JSON ENCODING UTF32)
--> X'5b 00 00 00 74 00 00 00 72 00 00 00 75 00 00 00 65 00 00 00 2c 00 00 00 31 00 00 00 5d 00 00 00'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_array # / Returned type #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT json_object('x' : true, 'y' : 12e-1, 'z' : 'text')
--> '{"x":true,"y":1.2,"z":"text"}'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_object # / Argument types #

evidence_span.text: Filtering during aggregation #

primary_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions #

evidence_span.text: The FILTER keyword can be used to remove rows from aggregation processing with a condition expressed using a WHERE clause. This is evaluated for each row before it is used in the aggregation and is supported for all aggregate functions.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions # / Filtering during aggregation #

evidence_span.text: aggregate_function(...) FILTER (WHERE <condition>)

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions # / Filtering during aggregation #

evidence_span.text: A common and very useful example is to use FILTER to remove nulls from consideration when using array_agg :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions # / Filtering during aggregation #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT array_agg(name) FILTER (WHERE name IS NOT NULL)
FROM region;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions # / Filtering during aggregation #

evidence_span.text: As another example, imagine you want to add a condition on the count for Iris flowers, modifying the following query:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions # / Filtering during aggregation #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT species,
       count(*) AS count
FROM iris
GROUP BY species;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions # / Filtering during aggregation #

evidence_span.text:
species    | count
-----------+-------
setosa     |   50
virginica  |   50
versicolor |   50

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions # / Filtering during aggregation #

evidence_span.text: If you just use a normal WHERE statement you lose information:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions # / Filtering during aggregation #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT species,
    count(*) AS count
FROM iris
WHERE petal_length_cm > 4
GROUP BY species;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions # / Filtering during aggregation #

evidence_span.text:
species    | count
-----------+-------
virginica  |   50
versicolor |   34

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions # / Filtering during aggregation #

evidence_span.text: Using a filter you retain all information:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions # / Filtering during aggregation #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT species,
       count(*) FILTER (where petal_length_cm > 4) AS count
FROM iris
GROUP BY species;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Aggregate functions # / Filtering during aggregation #

evidence_span.text:
species    | count
-----------+-------
virginica  |   50
setosa     |    0
versicolor |   34

evidence_span.text: json_table #

primary_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators #

evidence_span.text: The json_table clause extracts a table from a JSON value. Use this clause to transform JSON data into a relational format, making it easier to query and analyze. Use json_table in the FROM clause of a SELECT statement to create a table from JSON data.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
JSON_TABLE(
    json_input,
    json_path [ AS path_name ]
    [ PASSING value AS parameter_name [, ...] ]
    COLUMNS (
        column_definition [, ...] )
    [ PLAN ( json_table_specific_plan )
      | PLAN DEFAULT ( json_table_default_plan ) ]
    [ { ERROR | EMPTY } ON ERROR ]
)

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: The COLUMNS clause supports the following column_definition arguments:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
column_name FOR ORDINALITY
| column_name type
    [ FORMAT JSON [ ENCODING { UTF8 | UTF16 | UTF32 } ] ]
    [ PATH json_path ]
    [ { WITHOUT | WITH { CONDITIONAL | UNCONDITIONAL } } [ ARRAY ] WRAPPER ]
    [ { KEEP | OMIT } QUOTES [ ON SCALAR STRING ] ]
    [ { ERROR | NULL | EMPTY { [ARRAY] | OBJECT } | DEFAULT expression } ON EMPTY ]
    [ { ERROR | NULL | DEFAULT expression } ON ERROR ]
| NESTED [ PATH ] json_path [ AS path_name ] COLUMNS ( column_definition [, ...] )

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: json_input is a JSON value, a character string, or a binary string. A string must contain a single JSON item.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: json_path is a string literal containing the path mode specification and the path expression. It follows the syntax rules described in JSON path syntax and semantics .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
'strict ($.price + $.tax)?(@ > 99.9)'
'lax $[0 to 1].floor()?(@ > 10)'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: In the PASSING clause, pass values as named parameters that the json_path expression can reference.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
PASSING orders.totalprice AS o_price,
        orders.tax % 10 AS o_tax

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: Use named parameters to reference the values in the path expression. Prefix named parameters with $ .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: 'lax $?(@.price > $o_price || @.tax > $o_tax)'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: You can also pass JSON values in the PASSING clause. Use FORMAT JSON to specify the format and ENCODING to specify the encoding:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
PASSING orders.json_desc FORMAT JSON AS o_desc,
        orders.binary_record FORMAT JSON ENCODING UTF16 AS o_rec

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: The json_path value is case-sensitive. The SQL identifiers are uppercase. Use quoted identifiers in the PASSING clause:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
'lax $.keyvalue()?(@.name == $KeyName).value' PASSING nation.name AS KeyName --> ERROR; no passed value found
'lax $.keyvalue()?(@.name == $KeyName).value' PASSING nation.name AS "KeyName" --> correct

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: The PLAN clause specifies how to join columns from different paths. Use OUTER or INNER to define how to join parent paths with their child paths. Use CROSS or UNION to join siblings.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: COLUMNS defines the schema of your table. Each column_definition specifies how to extract and format your json_input value into a relational column.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: PLAN is an optional clause to control how to process and join nested JSON data.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: ON ERROR specifies how to handle processing errors. ERROR ON ERROR throws an error. EMPTY ON ERROR returns an empty result set.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: For each value column with DEFAULT in its ON EMPTY or ON ERROR clause, the default expression is only evaluated when the corresponding branch is taken, and if the ON EMPTY default itself raises a data exception, the failure cascades to the ON ERROR clause. Subqueries are not supported in json_table DEFAULT expressions.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: column_name specifies a column name.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: FOR ORDINALITY adds a row number column to the output table, starting at 1 . Specify the column name in the column definition:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: row_num FOR ORDINALITY

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: NESTED PATH extracts data from nested levels of a json_input value. Each NESTED PATH clause can contain column_definition values.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: The json_table function returns a result set that you can use like any other table in your queries. You can join the result set with other tables or combine multiple arrays from your JSON data.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: You can also process nested JSON objects without parsing the data multiple times.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: Use json_table as a lateral join to process JSON data from another table.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: Examples #

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: The following query uses json_table to extract values from a JSON array and return them as rows in a table with three columns:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table # / Examples #
JSON functions and operators # / json_table # / Examples #

evidence_span.text: id child wiki_data_id 1 Africa Q1 2 Americas Q828 3 Asia Q48 4 Europe Q51

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table # / Examples #

evidence_span.text: The json_table function returns a result set that you can use like any other table in your queries. You can join the result set with other tables or combine multiple arrays from your JSON data.
